title: The principles in an agile context
blurb: Explain how each PRINCE2 principle supports agile working, and recognize which principle an agile technique is serving.
question: A team shortens the feedback loop with its customer and holds a retrospective at the end of every iteration. Which PRINCE2 principle do these agile techniques support?

teach.body: PRINCE2 Agile does not invent new principles. It shows how each of the seven is applied, and often strengthened, when delivery is agile. Many agile techniques turn out to be ways of honouring a principle: retrospectives serve 'learn from experience', and prioritized backlogs serve 'focus on products'. All seven still apply in every PRINCE2 Agile project.

teach.h: How each principle looks in agile
head: Principle
In an agile context
rows: Value focus, MVP, project canvas, frequent releases
Short feedback loops, customer involvement, retrospectives
Add agile roles; tailor PRINCE2 roles carefully
Stages contain timeboxed releases and iterations
Tolerance on what is delivered, not on time or cost
Prioritize and decompose to flex what is delivered
Choose frameworks, artifacts and workshops; record in PID
teach.caption: Paraphrased from the V2 book Table 5.1 and section 5.2.

teach.h: Manage by exception: the heart of self-management
teach.body: PRINCE2 Agile calls manage by exception vital: it is at the heart of empowering people to self-manage while staying in control with the right level of governance. Working in an agile way means allowing tolerance on what is delivered and restricting tolerance on time and cost. Teams decide freely inside those limits and escalate only when a limit is forecast to be broken.

teach.h: Focus on products and learn from experience
teach.body: Focus on products: product descriptions, quality specifications and quality tolerances can be prioritized and decomposed, so what is delivered can flex while the project stays in control and focused on value. Learn from experience: many agile concepts support it, such as a shorter feedback loop to the customer, continual customer involvement, inspect and adapt, and retrospectives.

teach.h: Which principle does the technique serve?

teach.body: Pennine Rail Freight is building a booking portal. The team assigns value to each user story (business justification) and holds a retrospective after every iteration (learn from experience). A chief product owner and team coach are added alongside the PRINCE2 roles (roles). Releases sit inside stages (stages). The board fixes the go-live date and budget but lets the team trade Could-have features (exception). When agile maturity varies across teams, project manager Aisha Begum discusses it openly as a lesson rather than escalating it.

teach.text: Agile does not loosen the principles. In particular, manage by exception in agile restricts tolerance on time and cost and allows it on what is delivered, not the other way round. And differing agile maturity is handled transparently through lessons, not escalated as an exception unless tolerances are threatened.

items: All seven principles apply in PRINCE2 Agile; agile techniques help apply them.
Learn from experience: feedback loops, customer involvement, inspect and adapt, retrospectives.
Manage by exception: at the heart of self-management; tolerance on what is delivered, not on time and cost.
Focus on products: prioritize and decompose products and quality criteria to flex what is delivered.
Define roles: add agile roles and tailor PRINCE2 roles carefully.

summary: You can now explain how each principle is applied when delivery is agile. You can also link a technique, such as a retrospective or a prioritized backlog, to the principle it serves.

A.q: Which principle do retrospectives, a shorter feedback loop and continual customer involvement mainly support in PRINCE2 Agile?
A.why: Table 5.1 lists these as agile concepts supporting 'learn from experience'.

whyNot.0: Focus on products is supported by prioritizing and decomposing products to flex delivery.
whyNot.2: Manage by stages concerns stage-by-stage control with releases inside stages.
whyNot.3: Tailoring concerns choosing which agile frameworks, artifacts and workshops to use.

A.q: In an agile context, how does 'manage by exception' treat tolerances?
options: Tolerance on what is delivered; time and cost restricted
Tolerance on time and cost; what is delivered restricted
Tolerance on time; cost and what is delivered restricted
Tolerance on cost; time and what is delivered restricted
A.why: Working in an agile way allows tolerance on what is delivered and restricts tolerance on time and cost (Table 5.1).

whyNot.1: This reverses the agile emphasis: time and cost are the restricted aspects.
whyNot.2: Time has zero tolerance by default in PRINCE2 Agile.
whyNot.3: Cost has zero tolerance by default in PRINCE2 Agile.

A.q: Which principle is served when product descriptions and quality criteria are prioritized and decomposed so that what is delivered can flex?
A.why: Table 5.1 links prioritizing and decomposing product descriptions, quality specifications and tolerances to 'focus on products'.

whyNot.0: Learn from experience is supported by feedback loops and retrospectives.
whyNot.1: Manage by stages concerns stage-by-stage control.
whyNot.2: Business justification is supported by value focus and the MVP; the flexing of products is focus on products.

B.q: How does PRINCE2 Agile describe the 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' principle in an agile context?
options: PRINCE2 roles are replaced by the Scrum roles
Agile roles may be added and PRINCE2 roles tailored
Roles are agreed by each delivery team itself
Roles are fixed by the board for every iteration
B.why: Additional agile roles may be needed, and PRINCE2 roles should be tailored carefully to the agile context (Table 5.1).

whyNot.0: PRINCE2 roles are tailored, not replaced by another framework's roles.
whyNot.2: Roles are defined within PRINCE2 Agile's governance, not left wholly to teams.
whyNot.3: The board does not set roles iteration by iteration.

B.q: Delivery teams in a pilot show very different levels of agile maturity, but no tolerance is threatened. How should this be handled under PRINCE2 Agile?
options: Escalate it to the board as an exception
Raise a formal issue for the change authority
Handle it openly as lessons with the team
Pause the stage until all teams are equal
B.why: Varying agile maturity is handled transparently as lessons are gathered with the team; manage by exception applies only if tolerances are forecast to be exceeded (Table 5.1).

whyNot.0: Exceptions are for forecast tolerance breaches, which is not the case here.
whyNot.1: This is learning, not a request for change to a baseline.
whyNot.3: Differing maturity is a learning matter; it is no reason to halt delivery.

B.q: Which statement about manage by exception in PRINCE2 Agile is correct?
options: It is set aside so that teams can self-manage
It is replaced by daily stand-ups in each team
It applies at board level and not inside teams
It is at the heart of empowering self-management
B.why: Manage by exception is at the heart of empowering people to self-manage while staying in control with appropriate governance (Table 5.1).

whyNot.0: Self-management depends on it; it is not set aside.
whyNot.1: Stand-ups coordinate daily work; they do not replace tolerances.
whyNot.2: Tolerances cascade to all levels, including team plans.

C.q:
Which two statements are correct?
1. Retrospectives support the 'learn from experience' principle.
2. In agile, manage by exception allows tolerance on time and cost.
3. Agile roles may be added and PRINCE2 roles tailored under 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships'.
4. PRINCE2 Agile drops 'manage by stages' because it uses iterations.
C.why: Retrospectives support learn from experience (1), and agile roles may be added with PRINCE2 roles tailored (3) (Table 5.1).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: agile restricts tolerance on time and cost.
whyNot.1: Both are wrong: time and cost are restricted, and stages remain with iterations inside them.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is wrong: all seven principles still apply.

C.q: A board fixes the go-live date and budget, and lets the team drop Could-have features to meet them. Which principle is applied, and how?
options: Manage by exception: tolerance on what is delivered
Manage by stages: one release per stage authorized
Focus on products: products fixed, time flexed
Learn from experience: lessons drive the date
C.why: Restricting tolerance on time and cost and allowing it on what is delivered is manage by exception in an agile context (Table 5.1).

whyNot.1: The situation is about tolerances, not stage authorization.
whyNot.2: Products are flexed here, not fixed, and time is fixed.
whyNot.3: Lessons are not what fixes the date or flexes the scope.

C.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. Working in an agile way emphasizes allowing tolerance on what is delivered and restricting tolerance on time and [?].
C.why: Agile restricts tolerance on time and cost (Table 5.1); both have zero tolerance by default (Table 3.1).

whyNot.0: Quality criteria can be prioritized to flex what is delivered.
whyNot.1: Scope is part of what is delivered and is flexed for Should and Could haves.
whyNot.3: Benefits are fixed at minimum viability and flexed above it.

reteach.title: Agile techniques wearing PRINCE2 badges
reteach.question: How can an agile technique be evidence that a principle is being applied?

blocks.h: Match the habit to the principle
blocks.body: A retrospective is the team learning from experience. A prioritized backlog is focus on products in action. A fixed release date with flexible features is manage by exception. Valuing each story is continued business justification. Adding a chief product owner is defining roles. Choosing Kanban over Scrum and recording it in the PID is tailoring.

blocks.text: Time and cost are where agile is strict. What is delivered is where it is flexible.

explain.body: Supported by shortening the feedback loop, continual customer involvement, inspect and adapt, and retrospectives (Table 5.1).

test.q: Holding a retrospective at the end of each iteration is an agile way of applying which principle?
test.why: Retrospectives are listed as supporting 'learn from experience' (Table 5.1).

whyNot.2: Focus on products concerns well-defined, prioritized outputs.
whyNot.3: Manage by stages concerns stage-by-stage control.

explain.body: Restrict tolerance on time and cost; allow tolerance on what is delivered. Teams self-manage within those limits (Table 5.1).

test.q: Which aspect does agile working allow tolerance on, under manage by exception?
test.why: Agile allows tolerance on what is delivered and restricts it on time and cost (Table 5.1).

whyNot.3: A stage end date is time, which is restricted.

explain.body: Kept alive through a value focus, the MVP, the project canvas and frequent releases that can bring some benefits forward.

test.q: Which agile practice most directly supports 'ensure continued business justification'?
options: Assigning value to each user story
test.why: A value focus, such as assigning value to stories and prioritizing by value, keeps the project justified (6.3.1).

whyNot.1: Stand-ups coordinate daily work rather than test justification.
whyNot.3: A skill matrix maps team skills for training.

explain.body: Manage by stages: stages contain timeboxed releases and iterations. Tailor: choose agile frameworks, artifacts and workshops and record the tailoring in the PID.

test.q: A project manager records which agile framework, artifacts and workshops the project will use in the PID. Which principle is this?
test.why: Deciding and recording how agile frameworks, artifacts and workshops are used is tailoring to suit the project.

whyNot.0: Manage by stages concerns stage-by-stage control.
whyNot.1: Focus on products concerns well-defined outputs.
whyNot.2: Defining roles concerns who does what.
